column1: # Windows token privileges (whoami /priv, or the winPEAS token section) and how each is abused.
# The winprivesc detector pulls the SeXxxPrivilege token off a line, looks it up here, and reads
# the Enabled/Disabled state from the same line. Many service accounts (IIS, MSSQL) hold the
# impersonate privileges - those are the bread-and-butter SYSTEM escalations.
# severity  OK | INFO | NOTICE | WARN | CRITICAL
# technique short name of the attack a learner can go read up on

column4: description
Impersonate a client token. The classic service-account-to-SYSTEM path: coerce a SYSTEM auth and impersonate it. IIS/MSSQL/service accounts usually have this.
Assign a primary token to a new process - same SYSTEM escalation as SeImpersonate, via the Potato family.

column3: act as part of the OS
column4: Forge a token that includes SYSTEM/any group. Effectively full compromise.
Build an arbitrary access token (add SYSTEM/Administrators) and spawn a process with it.
Load a kernel driver. Load a known-exploitable signed driver and get ring-0 code execution.
Read ANY file ignoring its ACL - SAM, SYSTEM, NTDS.dit - then extract hashes offline (secretsdump).
Write ANY file or registry key - replace a service binary or utilman.exe/sethc.exe, or edit a service's ImagePath, for SYSTEM.
Take ownership of any securable object, then grant yourself full control and tamper with a SYSTEM binary or key.
Open any process. Dump LSASS for credentials (procdump/mimikatz) or inject into a SYSTEM process.
Full access to a volume: write anywhere (DLL hijack a SYSTEM service) and read raw sectors of SAM/SYSTEM, bypassing file ACLs.
Change the integrity label of objects - can be chained to tamper with higher-integrity resources.
Configure accounts as trusted for delegation - an Active Directory escalation primitive.
Manage auditing and the Security event log - cover tracks, and read some restricted objects.
Modify firmware environment values; niche, occasionally a persistence/EoP primitive.
Write to the security audit log; can be used to confuse monitoring.
Add machine accounts to the domain - useful in several AD attack chains.
Shut down the machine. Not an escalation on its own.
Shut down the machine remotely. Not an escalation on its own.
Bypass traverse checking. Held by everyone; benign.
Grow a process working set. Default and benign.
Change the time zone. Default and benign.
Undock a laptop. Benign.
Create global objects. Default for services; benign by itself.
Adjust process memory quotas. Benign.
Create a pagefile. Administrative but not an escalation primitive by itself.
Profile a single process. Low value on its own.
Profile system performance. Low value on its own.
